d8a.tech (pronounced "data tech") is an open source, warehouse-native web analytics pipeline. It receives the GA4 and Matomo tracking protocols, or its own web tracker, builds sessions on the backend, and writes clean, flat tables to BigQuery, ClickHouse or CSV/Parquet files. Run it in your own infrastructure, air-gapped if you need to, or use d8a.tech Cloud.

- **A flat, documented schema.** Events and sessions land as flat columns, ready for reporting, with no `UNNEST`. Custom parameters can be mapped to their own columns. Every column carries its own documentation, and the schema reference is generated from it.

- **Attribution and filtering.** Source and medium are derived from click IDs, referrers (search, social, email, video and AI assistants) and UTM parameters. Expression-based traffic filters exclude internal traffic or bots, with a test mode.
Timeline of one visit: events are collected as they happen, the session closes after the inactivity window, and events plus session columns are written to the warehouse at once

Receivers scale out; session processing runs on a single worker that scales vertically. The production operations guide documents roughly 7,000 requests per second (about 7 billion events a month) on a machine with 16 cores and 30 GB of RAM, and about 100 million events a month on 2 CPUs and 4 GB of RAM.
This repository is the full collection and processing pipeline. It ships without a reporting UI: bring your own BI tool, or start from the prebuilt Data Studio dashboard.

d8a.tech Cloud runs the same pipeline in the EU. The Cloud Dashboard plan adds a built-in analytics dashboard with goals, funnels and custom reports, plus Ask AI. The Cloud Warehouse plan writes to your own BigQuery or ClickHouse and comes with the prebuilt Data Studio dashboard. See pricing for the free tiers, the support package and Enterprise options.

`tls_cert` and `domain_expiry` use `warn_days` / `critical_days` thresholds and surface `days_remaining` plus registrar / cert subject in the result payload. Their floors are 1 hour for `tls_cert` and 12 hours for `domain_expiry`, regardless of plan — these probes track values that change on a scale of days, not minutes, and RDAP rate-limits by source address. `flow` runs a real browser, so it only executes where a browser engine is available (its regions clamp to the flow-capable set) and the number of flow monitors is capped per plan; put credentials in an org secret and reference them as `{{name}}`. Every flow run is kept with each step's outcome and duration, and the monitor page charts each step on its own scale, so a wait drifting from 200 ms to four seconds shows up long before the journey fails. **ClickHouse system logs are off.** Stock ClickHouse keeps two dozen `system.*_log` tables that grow without bound and use CPU at idle. Uptimepage reads none of them, so `config/clickhouse-quiet.xml` turns them all off; to get one back for debugging, delete its line there and run `docker compose up -d --force-recreate clickhouse` (a plain restart can keep reading the old file). A stack started before this setting existed keeps its old tables: run `docker compose up -d` first so ClickHouse restarts with the setting, then list them with `SELECT name, formatReadableSize(total_bytes) FROM system.tables WHERE database = 'system' AND name LIKE '%\_log%'` and remove each with `DROP TABLE system.<name>`.

Zero-config anomaly detection for your database tables.
No YAML, no rules, no thresholds. Scherlok learns what "normal" looks like, then tells you when something changes.
|**Distribution shift**|Column mean of a numeric column shifted 3+ standard deviations (Shewhart-style control limit) and at least 1%|INFO, WARNING above 5σ|
|**Cardinality explosion**|Status column went from 5 values to 500|CRITICAL|
|**Broken new table**|First sighting, no baseline yet: the table is empty, a column is NULL in every row, or its `id` / ` _id` has duplicates|WARNING (CRITICAL under `verify --table`)|
|**Constant column**|First sighting: one value in 100+ non-NULL rows|INFO|

Scherlok profiles every table: row counts, column types, NULL rates, value distributions, freshness cadence, cardinality. Stores everything locally in SQLite, as aggregates only: no value from your rows is saved (what Scherlok stores).

The connection is passed through the environment and masked, the comment never holds a value read from a row, and fork pull requests, which get no secrets, are skipped with a notice. 📖 GitHub Action guide →

Tables without a baseline are listed under `tables_without_baseline`, never counted as verified. Those you name with `--table` count as just built: an empty table, a column NULL in every row or a duplicate key there is CRITICAL, so an agent can gate on a table it just created. Every `watch`, `ci`, `check` and `verify` run is recorded, passing or not: `scherlok history --runs` lists them. Every anomaly in the JSON also carries `column`, `metric`, `baseline`, `current`, `change_pct` and a fixed `hint`, so it can be acted on without parsing the message. 📖 CI/CD gate guide →

It reports `row_count_mismatch`, `duplicate_keys` (a key repeated in the target: join fan-out), `missing_keys`, `extra_keys` and `sum_mismatch` (totals apart by more than the absolute `--tolerance`), all CRITICAL, with `--output json` for CI. It needs no baseline and saves nothing, and it reports counts and totals only, never a key value. On BigQuery and Snowflake every run scans both tables in full. 📖 Reconcile guide →

**This is a guardrail, not a security boundary.** An agent with shell access can run `scherlok accept` or edit the SQLite file itself. Real enforcement means running `verify` in CI against a store the agent has no credentials for, with `accept` run from a workflow a person triggers. 📖 Accepting a change →

It changes only *where the symbols come from*, not *which backends exist*: `mysql.h` / `libpq-fe.h` / `sql.h` are still needed at configure time (`MYSQL_BIND`'s layout has to come from the real header), so `UVCPP_DB_MYSQL_ENABLE` / `UVCPP_DB_PGSQL_ENABLE` / `UVCPP_DB_ODBC_ENABLE` still mean "the header was found". Default `OFF` leaves today's behaviour byte-for-byte. See `doc/db-guide.md`|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_REDIS`|`ON`|Enable the **Redis client** (`src/redis/`): built-in RESP2/RESP3, asynchronous over `uvcpp_tcp_client`, with AUTH / SELECT / pipelines / pub-sub / `HELLO 3` / `rediss://`. **No third-party client library is needed** (not hiredis), which is why it is on by default; it depends on the net module and is force-disabled when `UVCPP_BUILD_NET=OFF`. See `doc/redis-guide.md`|
|`UVCPP_BUILD_LIBUV_FROM_SOURCE`|`OFF`|Fetch and build libuv from source via `FetchContent`|

|`UVCPP_STATIC_RUNTIME`|`OFF`|Statically link the compiler runtime (`libgcc`/`libstdc++`) into the library. **MinGW and Linux only — a no-op on MSVC**, which uses `/MD` and ships `vcruntime`/`msvcp` in the package. **On Linux it also applies to every executable, and a *shared* `libuvcpp.so` built with it cannot be combined with a consumer that uses the system `libstdc++.so.6`** — both copies instantiate the same COMDAT templates (`std::once_flag`'s `__once_proxy`, `std::__future_base::_State_baseV2`) and ELF's global symbol scope makes one side jump into the other's frame, so the failure is a run-time segfault or `double free`, **not a link error**. **That is why the release workflow's two Linux legs no longer pass it** (1.7.0 onwards) — the Linux packages therefore need the system `libstdc++.so.6` / `libgcc_s.so.1`, which every distro with a C++ runtime already has. The two MinGW legs still pass it: PE has no global symbol scope, so there is nothing to interpose, and a MinGW user's machine may not have `libstdc++-6.dll`. See `doc/build-guide.md`|
|`UVCPP_ENABLE_TRY_WRITE`|`ON`|Try `uv_try_write` before copying into a write buffer|
|`UVCPP_TRY_WRITE_MIN_BYTES`|`32768`|Smallest payload worth attempting `uv_try_write` for (a `CACHE STRING`, not an `option()`)|

|`UVCPP_ENABLE_UDP_GSO`|`ON` when Windows **and** `UVCPP_ENABLE_QUIC=ON`, else `OFF`|Send-side UDP Segmentation Offload for the QUIC transport: hand a batch of equal-sized datagrams to the stack in **one** `WSASendTo` via `UDP_SEND_MSG_SIZE`, instead of one syscall per datagram. The segment size is taken from what each aggregate write reports, so the wire carries exactly the datagrams it carries today. **Windows only** — the code is compiled out elsewhere and the switch is a no-op there. See `doc/quic-guide.md`|
